title: Count Key Switches
statement:
Someone typed the string s, made of upper- and lowercase English letters. A key switch happens when a letter is typed on a different key than the letter just before it.

Shift and Caps Lock do not count: "q" and "Q" are the same key. Return the number of key switches.

examples.why: a → A and b → B stay on one key. Only A → b is a switch. A case-sensitive comparison would wrongly count 3.
Every step moves to the other key. Counting distinct keys would give 2: switches are about neighbors, not about how many keys were used.
All four letters are on the Z key.

hints: A switch is decided by two neighboring letters only.
Before comparing two letters, bring them to the same case.
Count i from 1 to n − 1 where lowercase(s[i]) differs from lowercase(s[i − 1]).

explain.intuition: Whether a switch happens at position i depends only on s[i − 1] and s[i], so one pass over neighboring pairs is enough. The only twist is that case must not matter. Normalize first, for instance with toLowerCase(), the same way you would before comparing user-entered tags.
steps: Lowercase the string once (or each letter as you compare it).
For i from 1 to n − 1, add 1 when t[i] ≠ t[i − 1].
pitfalls: Comparing letters case-sensitively, which counts a → A as a switch.
Counting distinct keys instead of changes between neighbors: "abab" uses 2 keys but has 3 switches.

complexity.space: O(n) for the lowercased copy, O(1) if you compare letter by letter

solutions.title: Lowercase, then compare neighbors
solutions.idea: Normalize the case of the whole string, then count positions where a letter differs from the one before it.

solutions.title: Compare codes with the case bit cleared
solutions.idea: In ASCII, upper- and lowercase letters differ only in bit 5 (value 32). Clearing that bit maps both cases to the same code without building a new string.

followups: The string also contains digits and symbols, and Shift turns 1 into ! on the same key. How would you model which characters share a key?
Count the number of maximal runs typed on one key instead. How does it relate to the number of switches?
